title: Come, my beloved
hookLine: Shlomo Alkabetz's song greets Shabbat as a bride; everyone turns to the door at the end
tomorrow: A good thing to give thanks (Psalm 92:2)

lines: EVERY HEAD TURNS TO THE DOOR.
cards: At a wedding, every head turns toward the back when the doors open for the bride. On Friday night in a synagogue, the same thing happens with no one at the door. A song has been building, verse after verse.
At the last verse, the congregation stands, turns around, and faces the doors at the back. Some bow. Nobody walks in.
Nobody needs to. The guest they're turning to greet is the Sabbath, arriving like a bride.

teach.h: COME, MY BELOVED, MEET THE BRIDE.
teach.b: Lecha dodi means come, my beloved. The refrain goes: come, my beloved, to meet the bride; let us welcome the face of Shabbat. It was written by Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz, one of the kabbalists of Safed from yesterday.

teach.h: ALKABETZ SIGNED IT IN THE LETTERS.
teach.b: He signed it, in a way: the first letters of the first eight verses spell his name, Shlomo Halevi. The words are made almost entirely of older words. Come, my beloved, comes from the Song of Songs.
In the old Jewish translation: "Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field." And the bride comes from the Talmud. Yesterday's sage greeted Shabbat as a queen.
Another, Rabbi Yannai, put on his Sabbath clothes and said: come, O bride, come, O bride. Then the song turns. Its middle verses aren't about Shabbat at all.
They speak to Jerusalem, as if to a city lying in the dust. Shake off the dust, arise.
Wake up, wake up, your light has come. A song of hope that the broken will be rebuilt, set inside the welcome of a single day.
Then the final verse: come in peace, crown of her husband, ending with that line from the Talmud, come, O bride, come, O bride.
That's when everyone turns. Tradition says the kabbalists of Safed sang it out in the fields, facing the setting sun. Indoors, the room faces the door instead.
A welcome that once meant walking out now means turning around.

how: Lecha Dodi is sung in the Friday evening service after the six psalms of Kabbalat Shabbat; at the last verse the congregation stands, turns to face the entrance, and many bow at 'come, O bride'. Mourners in their first week often enter at this point and are greeted.

o: come, my beloved: a song greeting Shabbat as a bride
a blessing said under the canopy at a wedding
a love poem from the Song of Songs, sung whole

games.q: inside Lecha Dodi — tap the pairs.

s: Lecha Dodi is only about Shabbat
its middle verses speak to Jerusalem: shake off the dust, arise.
the author's name is hidden in the verses
the first letters spell Shlomo Halevi.
the congregation turns toward the door at the last verse
to greet Shabbat arriving like a bride.

games.q: you're in a synagogue on Friday night. Lecha Dodi reaches its last verse: come, O bride. what do you do?
o: stand, turn to face the door, and bow.
games.why: everyone turns to face the door, greeting Shabbat the bride. tradition says Safed's kabbalists faced the setting sun.

practice: Stand if you can, turn slowly to face the door of the room you're in, and picture something good about to come through it, not a person you're waiting on, but rest, quiet, peace.
If you know the words, say come, O bride, softly; if not, just say come in, and bow a little if you like.

wordCard.voice: Lecha dodi. Come, my beloved. The Safed song that greets Shabbat as a bride, and turns the whole room to the door.

orig.note: Hebrew: come, my beloved, from Song of Songs 7:12.

carryVoice: Your line: shake off the dust, arise. Even a city in the dust gets a verse of hope. Six hundred fifteen days now.
